claims.text: The state of the native oxide film controls corrosion protection in Q235 steel.
At room temperature, slow oxidation kinetics permit formation of a uniform, adherent, protective passive film on Q235 steel.
The room-temperature passive film limits metal degradation.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C transforms the native film into a porous, less-adherent oxide scale.
Accelerated oxidation at microstructural defects drives the high-temperature transformation of the oxide film.
A porous, poorly adherent high-temperature oxide scale permits rapid oxidation and corrosion.
As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide film.
As-received Q235 steel contains microstructural defects such as grain boundaries and inclusions.
Pre-annealing can modify the grain size and defect density of Q235 steel.
The density, porosity, and adhesion of the oxide layer are modulated by the distribution of defects in the Q235 microstructure.
At room temperature, limited oxidation produces a continuous passive film that retards further metal-ion diffusion.
At high temperature, grain boundaries and inclusions promote rapid oxidation.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, high-temperature salt exposure will cause greater mass change in Q235 steel.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, high-temperature salt exposure will cause greater surface degradation.
The high-temperature oxide scale will be more porous and less adherent than the room-temperature passive film.
Room-temperature salt exposure is expected to produce minimal mass change and preserve an intact, adherent passive oxide film.
Additional alloying elements or engineered surface treatments may stabilize the oxide layer at high temperature and make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
A high-temperature film that remains as continuous, dense, and adherent as the room-temperature film, with minimal mass change and no defect-facilitated oxidation, would falsify the hypothesis.
